hero.lede: PowerBGInfo puts machine details, charts, tables and diagrams on desktop and lock-screen wallpapers. You describe the layout in PowerShell or JSON and bring the data; ChartForgeX draws the whole image, from the generated backdrop to the last chart label.
hero.alt: Server status wallpaper rendered by PowerBGInfo: the host name SQL-PROD-01 with its role and owner, four tiles for uptime, CPU, memory and network, and panels for volumes, network throughput and critical services.

scenarios.title: Twelve wallpapers, each with one job
scenarios.body: Each script answers one question for the person in front of the screen, and each renders in light and dark at any resolution. A theme preset gives each its look and regions place the panels. Every script starts with a data block of fixed samples, so anyone can reproduce the renders, and a comment beside each value names the command that supplies it on a real machine. Three are shown in full here, with the New-BGInfo call that draws each one and the data block it reads.

more.title: More wallpapers
more.body: Filter by who the screen is for. Each card opens the wallpaper in the page theme with the same Presentation and Data tabs, and links to the full-size PNG and the script on GitHub.

screens.title: Any screen
screens.body: A script lays out for the screen it renders on. The on-call board spreads across a 3440 x 1440 ultrawide in the operations room, and the signage script turns a 1080 x 1920 portrait panel into a poster. Each file is drawn at its size, not scaled from 1920 x 1080.

build.title: Build one yourself
build.body: One wallpaper in eight steps. Each step shows only the lines it changes, next to the wallpaper the whole script renders at that point. Every background is generated: there is no stock image underneath, only a gradient, glows and a pattern that ChartForgeX paints at the screen's size.
build.alt: Wallpaper for WS-FIN-0042 after the step

backdrop.title: Generate the background in layers
backdrop.body: Three keys on the same hashtable add one layer each. The backdrop is painted at the size you ask for, so it is never a stretched photo.

logic.title: Your logic, your data
logic.body: Collecting the values is the part only you can write, so PowerBGInfo keeps it apart from the drawing. Every example has the same two regions: a data block that returns plain values, and a presentation block that only reads them.

data.title: The data block
data.body: One function returns one object. This is where your sources go: replace the sample values, keep the property names, and the layout keeps working. A comment beside each value names a live source for it.

sources.title: Typical sources
sources.body: Each snippet is a body for that function. Combine them as you need; the wallpaper only sees the object they return.

safety.title: A slow source never blocks logon
safety.body: Invoke-BGInfoDataSource runs your function in its own runspace with a time limit. When the function throws, returns nothing or runs out of time, it writes a warning and returns the fallback you gave it, so the wallpaper always renders and sign-in never waits on a broken CMDB.
points: Keep -TimeoutSeconds small, 5 to 15 seconds. A timed-out runspace is stopped in the background and the call returns at the limit.
The function cannot see your script's variables. Pass what it needs with -ArgumentList and read it with param().
Give each slow source its own call, so one failure only replaces its own values.

swap.title: Swap a built-in helper
swap.body: Get-BGInfoSystemInfo returns uptime, OS and build, IPv4, fixed disks, the last update, Defender and BitLocker state and the console user as one plain object, and every probe in it is read-only. A function of your own that returns the same property names replaces it; the system facts example does exactly that with sample values.
swap.tokens: The same facts are built-in tokens for New-BGInfoValue -BuiltinValue:
swap.alt: System facts wallpaper for WS-ANALYST-11 rendered from sample values with the same property names as Get-BGInfoSystemInfo: signed-in user, Windows build, uptime, IP address and last update, a protection list and a disks table.

capabilities.title: Themes, regions and widgets
capabilities.body: Six theme presets give a wallpaper one look in one parameter, five regions lay it out on any screen, and eight widget cmdlets draw what charts alone cannot.

themes.title: Six theme presets
themes.body: Each preset has a light and a dark pair; the page theme picks which one you see. New-BGInfoTheme adjusts a preset's accent, scale or font, and parameters you set always win.

regions.title: Regions on every screen
regions.body: One script rendered at three sizes. Left and Right are columns, Top and Bottom are bands and Center sits between them; a panel without a size shares what is left. New-BGInfoLayout keeps the taskbar and the desktop icons clear.

widgets.title: Widgets
widgets.body: Each widget is one cmdlet that takes plain values, hashtables or the pipeline, and flows into a region like any chart. The crops come from the feature examples; open one for the whole wallpaper.

parts.title: What ChartForgeX draws
parts.body: PowerBGInfo collects the values, lays out the wallpaper and applies it through Windows. Every pixel of the image comes from ChartForgeX; there is no System.Drawing or browser underneath. A theme preset resolves into the same ChartForgeX light or dark mode for every part, so a wallpaper reads as one design instead of a stack of overlays.

items.title: Charts
items.body: Thirteen chart kinds, from sparklines and gauges to progress bars and pictorial rows. Thresholds colour each bar, row or gauge by its value.

start.title: Get started
start.body: Install the module from the PowerShell Gallery and render to a file first, so you can check the layout before anything changes on a desktop.

production.title: Run it in production
production.body: PowerBGInfo has no refresh schedule of its own: each run renders the image, applies it once and exits. To keep the values current, run it again at sign-in, at unlock or on a timer, from the tool that already manages the machines.

routes.when: Standalone machines and labs, or any fleet where another tool runs the registration script once. The most direct way to refresh at sign-in, at unlock and on a timer, in the user's own session.

Active Directory domain-joined PCs and session hosts. A Group Policy Preferences task runs it for each user, and the same GPO can carry the execution policy and, on Enterprise and Education, the lock screen policy.

Microsoft Entra joined or hybrid joined devices. A Win32 app installs the module and the script and registers the per-user task; platform scripts, Remediations and the Personalization CSP cover the cases around it.
Devices managed by Configuration Manager, including co-managed devices where the apps workload stays with it. An application installs the module and registers the same task.

Session hosts and AVD multi-session run the task in every session, with a per-user output folder and a fresh render on reconnect; LoggedOnUser names the user of the session being rendered. AVD personal desktops and Cloud PCs work like a physical PC.

notes.title: What needs admin
notes.body: Setting your own wallpaper and -Target File need no elevation. -AllUsers, -Target LogonScreen and -Target Both do, and so do installing the module for all users and registering a task for every user or for SYSTEM, once per machine. Run the wallpaper task itself as a limited user.

notes.title: Signing
notes.body: Evotec signs its module releases with Authenticode. Under the AllSigned execution policy, add the publisher's certificate to Trusted Publishers so an unattended task never stops at a prompt, and sign your own wallpaper script with your code-signing certificate.

notes.title: Every monitor
notes.body: Get-BGInfoMonitor returns each monitor's index, device name, primary flag, bounds and scale (-Primary returns only the main one), needs no elevation and works under Constrained Language Mode. Loop over it, pass -MonitorIndex and give each monitor its own -OutputFileName, as Examples/Run.BGInfo.PerMonitor.ps1 does. PowerBGInfo never draws on its own earlier output, so repeated runs do not stack the text.
notes.guideTitle: Monitors and files in the production guide

notes.title: Keeping logon fast
notes.body: Prefer a scheduled task to a synchronous logon script, so the desktop never waits. Time-box each data source at 5 to 15 seconds; Get-BGInfoSystemInfo already limits each of its queries to five. Give the task an execution time limit so a stuck run cannot pile up.
